 Teachers union sues education secretary over public service loan forgiveness delays
 BY 
 Susan Carpenter 
 Nationwide 
 PUBLISHED 2:04 PM ET Oct. 30, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 2:04 PM EDT Oct. 30, 2026 
 SHARE 
 The American Federation of Teachers filed a class action lawsuit Friday against Education Secretary Linda McMahon alleging she systematically prevented over 90,000 borrowers from receiving public service loan forgiveness as required by law.
 The lawsuit claims borrowers who applied for debt relief have not received information on the status of their applications, requiring them to continue making payments they thought would be forgiven.
 “Teachers, nurses and first responders give up higher pay to serve their communities,” AFT President Randi Weingarten said at a news conference in Boston on Friday announcing the lawsuit, in which she is named as the lead plaintiff. “They held up their part of the bargain. The federal government has not.”
 Republican President George W. Bush first signed the bipartisan Public Service Loan Forgiveness program into law in 2007, enabling teachers, nurses, first responders and other qualifying public service workers to have their student loan balances canceled after they made 120 monthly payments.
 Because of changes to federal repayment plans, some of which took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, the U.S. Education Department and loan servicers placed some borrowers into deferment or forbearance for several months. A buyback provision that allowed borrowers to pay the deferred amounts and have them credited to the 120-payment total has been backlogged during the second Trump administration, the lawsuit alleges.
 In April 2025, 49,000 borrowers applied to participate in the buyback — a number that grew to 90,000 by April 2026, the AFT said. The lawsuit alleges McMahon’s deliberate mismanagement has led to those applications being shelved, preventing them from receiving the loan forgiveness.
 The Education Department did not respond to Spectrum News’ request for comment about the lawsuit before this story was published.
 Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., a senior member of the Senate Education Committee, said at the AFT news conference that the loan forgiveness program has delivered $96 billion in relief to nearly 1.3 million public servants since it was launched. But he said the Education Department is working to debilitate the program.
 He criticized the department’s alleged practice of rescinding loan payment credits that had been deemed eligible — one of several contentions also made in the lawsuit.
 “Many borrowers can’t even see their current payment count because it hasn’t even been updated since July. At Linda McMahon’s former job at World Wrestling Federation, they called that a clothesline or a body slam,” Markey said, referencing McMahon’s former position as CEO of World Wrestling Entertainment. “But in real life, you know what we call it? It’s illegal.”
 In the case filed in federal District Court for the District of Columbia on Friday, the AFT contends the Education Department has also withheld recently earned qualifying Public Service Loan Forgiveness payments without offering explanations to borrowers.
 David Petley, a board-certified critical care pharmacist who works for a not-for-profit hospital in rural Oregon, said Friday that it was the loan forgiveness program that drew him to a job that required a pay cut.
 “I’ve now worked at my rural hospital for more than 11 years,” said Petley, who is a co-plaintiff in the lawsuit and an associate AFT member.
 For part of his employment, he said, his student loan was placed into involuntary forbearance that he applied to buy back on May 1, 2025, the first day he was eligible, but he hasn’t heard anything from the Education Department.
 “This uncertainty has real financial consequences,” he said. “My monthly loan payments are now over 70% higher than the payments owed for the months that I’m seeking to buy back.”
 The lawsuit alleges the Education Department has failed to give borrowers the loan payment credits they earned by working in public service and illegally withheld and delayed buyback determinations.
 The lawsuit is asking the court to compel the Education Department to forgive the loans of all borrowers who meet the Public Service Loan Forgiveness requirements as required under the Higher Education Act.
